response.text:
Short answer
- You remain liable for fees that have been accrued through the effective date of termination. In other words, termination for convenience does not eliminate payment obligations for fees earned/owed up to the termination's effective date.

Quoted text you can use in the memo
- Page 4, §3.2: "either party may terminate for convenience upon ninety days written notice."
- Page 11, §7.1: "termination for convenience does not relieve customer of fees accrued through the effective date."

Plain-language interpretation (for the memo)
- §3.2 lets either party end the agreement for convenience, but it requires 90 days' written notice—so termination will typically become effective 90 days after you give notice.
- §7.1 says that termination for convenience does not relieve the customer of fees accrued through the effective date. That means you must pay all fees that have been incurred/earned by the vendor up to the date the termination takes effect (i.e., the termination effective date). This generally includes invoices already issued and any fees for services performed or committed through that effective date.

Practical implications / scenarios
- If you give the required 90‑day notice and continue to receive services during the notice period, you will owe fees for those 90 days (and any other fees that accrue up to the effective date).
- If you try to stop using the service immediately without giving the required notice, you risk breach and potentially additional liability beyond the "accrued fees" (depending on other MSA provisions). Do not assume immediate cessation avoids payment.
- If you pre‑paid for future services, check the MSA for refund/credit language—§7.1 does not by itself say whether prepayments are refundable; it only preserves the customer's obligation to pay fees accrued through the effective date.

What to check next in the MSA (quote these sections in your memo if present)
- Definitions: how is "effective date" defined? (Sometimes defined as the date termination becomes effective; confirm.)
- Fees / Payment / Invoicing: definition of "fees", billing frequency, when fees are considered "accrued," payment terms, late fees.
- Refunds / Credits / Prepayment: whether vendor must refund unused prepaid fees or will apply them to the final invoice.
- Remedies / Breach / Damages / Liquidated Damages: whether termination without proper notice triggers additional charges.
- Statement(s) of Work (SOWs) or Order Forms: SOWs can include their own termination/payment mechanics.
- Suspension / Stop Work / Transition Services: obligations during wind‑down that could generate additional fees.

Suggested short memo language (copy/paste)
- "Per the MSA, 'either party may terminate for convenience upon ninety days written notice.' (MSA, p.4, §3.2). The agreement further states that 'termination for convenience does not relieve customer of fees accrued through the effective date.' (MSA, p.11, §7.1). Therefore, if we terminate for convenience we will remain responsible for all fees incurred or earned by the vendor through the effective date of termination (i.e., the date the termination takes effect). We should confirm the MSA's definitions of 'effective date' and 'fees' and review invoicing/prepayment provisions to determine any final amounts, refunds, or additional liabilities."

Recommended next steps
1. Confirm how "effective date" and "accrued" are defined in the MSA.
2. Pull invoices and service records to calculate fees that will have accrued through the effective date (if you plan to give 90 days' notice, calculate through that future date).
3. Search the MSA for refund/prepayment language and any early-termination damages or breach remedies.
4. Consider giving the required written notice (if you plan to terminate) to avoid breach exposure; have legal review before sending.

Note: I’m not a lawyer. For binding legal advice or to prepare and send termination notice, have your legal team review the full MSA and final memo.
